column3: Is LiveReview adoption increasing?
column7: Area = reviews; line = 7-day rolling avg; rule = target
column8: More informative than a plain line. The rolling average shows whether adoption is genuinely increasing rather than being driven by noisy days.
column9: Is LiveReview adoption increasing since my team started using it?

column3: Are engineers actually incorporating reviews into their daily workflow?
column8: Gives a very immediate “usage rhythm.” Weekday gaps, isolated users, and sudden changes become visually obvious. Particularly good for a 14–30 day trial.
column9: Are engineers actually incorporating reviews into their daily workflow since my team started using it?

column3: How broadly has the organization adopted LiveReview?
column8: Shows whether usage is broad or concentrated. “500 reviews” means something very different if one engineer generated 450.

column3: Who has adopted LiveReview—and who hasn't?
column8: Rank engineers from highest to lowest. Add a vertical target rule, e.g. 5 reviews/day. This is directly actionable for engineering leaders.
column9: Who has adopted LiveReview the most and least?

column3: Is adoption becoming broader over time?
column8: This is much more interesting than total users. It answers whether the organization is moving from “a few enthusiasts” toward habitual adoption.

column3: Which repositories are gaining or losing engineering velocity?
column7: One line per repository; color = gain/loss
column8: Probably one of your strongest CTO charts. It makes period-over-period movement immediately visible. Label only the biggest movers.

column3: Where is organizational velocity concentrated?
column8: Answers “are our top 3 repos responsible for 80% of activity?” This reveals concentration and organizational risk.

column3: Which repositories are unusually active or inactive?
column8: Separates high-volume/high-frequency repos from large-diff/low-frequency repos. Add quadrant rules. Very useful for identifying anomalous teams.

column3: What does engineering activity look like across repositories and days?
column8: This is excellent for finding bursts, sustained inactivity, and velocity dips. Add text only for unusually high/low cells.

column3: What happened to a repository's velocity?
column4: Layered line + rolling average + highlighted interval
column7: Line = daily LOC; second line = rolling avg; rectangle = selected period
column8: Directly implements your 6.1 idea while using Vega-Lite's layering/annotation capabilities.

column3: Why did this repository's velocity change?
column8: Compare previous vs current period per engineer. It turns “velocity dropped 30%” into “Alice -40%, Bob -20%, Carol +5%.”

column3: Which engineers are carrying the repository?
column7: X = LOC; Y = contributor; point size = reviews
column8: Better than bars when you want to show the distribution and outliers. Particularly useful when there are many engineers.

column3: What does each engineer actually spend their review activity on?
column8: Small multiples let a CTO see whether an engineer is concentrated on one repo or spreading across many. Vega-Lite supports trellis/faceted views.

column3: Where are reviews happening?
column7: Color = trigger: PR/MR, pre-commit, MCP, API, manual
column8: More useful than a pie chart because you can compare periods. The key question is whether activity is migrating toward earlier review stages.

column3: Are we moving review earlier in the development lifecycle?
column8: Shows the transition between workflows. This is strategically more interesting than simply showing source distribution.

column3: Are serious issues being caught before PR/MR?
column8: Rows = pre-commit, PR/MR, MCP, API; columns = critical/high/medium/low. A leader can immediately see whether serious findings are disproportionately arriving late.

column3: What kinds of engineering problems is LiveReview finding?
column7: Rectangle area = finding count; color = severity
column8: Excellent for “what is LR actually discovering?” Use hierarchy category → subcategory. Requires reliably extracting category/severity from ai_comments.content, since the schema stores the comment payload as JSON rather than a normalized issue-category column.

column3: Where are the issues concentrated?
column8: The ai_comments.file_path field makes file-level concentration directly possible. Show only top files per repo.

column3: What is the blast radius of issues being caught?
column8: Each bubble = review or issue cluster. Large/high-severity bubbles in the upper-right are the reviews where LR prevented potentially large problems. File-level blast radius is supported by ai_comments.file_path; dependency-level blast radius would require additional metadata.

column3: How much does LiveReview save versus alternatives?
column7: Positive = avoided cost; negative = LR cost
column8: Start with hypothetical alternative cost, subtract LR LLM cost + subscription, arrive at net savings. Vega-Lite explicitly has a waterfall example.

column3: How much code has LR reviewed?
column8: Extremely compact long-term view. Useful when the dashboard needs to show 30–90 days without consuming much space. Vega-Lite has a native horizon-graph pattern.

column3: Are reviews getting faster?
column8: A CTO cares less about average latency than whether the tail is becoming problematic. Layered/error-band techniques are well supported.

column3: How much engineering work is being covered by LR?
column8: Add a derived LOC/review tooltip. This distinguishes more reviews from genuinely more code being inspected.

column3: Are reviews becoming more iterative?
column8: Distribution is more revealing than an average. A long right tail means some commits are being reviewed repeatedly.

column3: Which engineers are getting the most value from LR?
column8: Separates “heavy users” from “productive users.” If feedback is sufficiently populated, this can become one of the most interesting charts.

column3: Are people trusting the reviews?
column8: review_feedback explicitly records up/down votes and severity, so this is grounded in the schema.

column3: Which repositories have the highest review coverage?
column8: Useful if you can establish total changed LOC/PRs from the Git-host data. This distinguishes high LR usage from genuinely broad coverage.

column3: What does a healthy engineering-review workflow look like?
column8: Plot successive weekly states and connect them. The trajectory itself becomes meaningful: more pre-commit reviews + lower latency + fewer late critical findings. Connected scatterplots are explicitly supported by Vega-Lite.
column11: review_feedback.severity has only 15 rows total across ~10 weeks - too sparse to plot a meaningful weekly trajectory.

column3: How much of the organization's activity is covered by the top users?
column8: Makes “adoption is broad” vs “three people are doing everything” immediately apparent.

column3: What changed between week 1 and week 2?
column8: Rows = reviews, LOC, active engineers, repos, pre-commit %, critical findings, etc. Columns = W1/W2/delta. This can become a compact “14-day verdict.”
